metaDescription: Auburn, WV mineral owner sitting on old Ritchie County oil paper or a Marcellus lease? We buy fractional interests, heir shares, and flat-rate leases directly.
heroLead: Auburn is Ritchie County oil country in the literal sense, close enough to the old Burning Springs field that some tracts here were leased before the county even had a courthouse fire to lose the records to.
intro: Ritchie County was drilling shallow oil wells before most of the United States knew what a mineral lease was, and Auburn's ownership history reflects it: layered leases, some from the 1890s boom and some from the 2000s Marcellus rush, sitting on top of each other on the same tract.

We buy mineral and royalty interests around Auburn as they actually sit in the chain of title, whether that means a modern Marcellus unit share, a legacy shallow-well royalty, or an old flat-rate lease that was never converted.

sections.heading: Two eras of drilling on one tract
paragraphs: It's routine in this part of Ritchie County to find a Big Injun or Gordon sand well from the early twentieth century still nominally producing on the same parcel that later got pulled into a modern Marcellus or Utica/Point Pleasant unit. Both can generate royalty at once, on completely different lease terms, which is exactly why we read the actual recorded instruments rather than assume one lease governs everything.

sections.heading: Flat-rate leases and the conversion statute
paragraphs: West Virginia law requires flat-rate gas leases to convert to a minimum one-eighth royalty on production, but that conversion only happens if someone applies it. A lot of legacy Ritchie County leases were never updated, and heirs sometimes keep collecting the same small flat payment their grandparents got in 1955. We check whether your lease qualifies for conversion before we price an interest.

sections.heading: Heirship fragmentation around Auburn
paragraphs: Family farms in this stretch of Ritchie County were often split among four or five children a generation ago, then split again. It's not unusual for a mineral tract near Auburn to have a dozen record owners, several out of state, a few deceased without a will filed. We buy individual heir shares without requiring the whole family to agree or sell together.

faqs.question: How do I know if my Auburn lease is a flat-rate lease?
faqs.answer: Look at the recorded lease in the Ritchie County Clerk's office. If it specifies a fixed dollar amount per well per year rather than a royalty percentage, it's a flat-rate lease and may be eligible for conversion.

faqs.question: Can two different companies both owe me royalty on the same land?
faqs.answer: Yes, if there's a legacy shallow well and a separate modern deep unit on the same tract, each operator pays under its own lease or unit order, and the two payments are tracked separately.

faqs.question: Do I need to probate my parents' estate before selling their share?
faqs.answer: Not always. We can often structure a purchase around heir interests directly, though a clean chain of title does make closing faster.

faqs.question: Will you buy a very small fractional interest?
faqs.answer: Yes. We regularly buy fractional interests down to a small percentage of a divided tract, provided the title can be reasonably traced.
